paragraphs: Newton's method uses second-order information to guide optimization, but choosing how far to move is important for convergence. This paper introduces a step-size schedule that gives the method both a fast global convergence guarantee and quadratic convergence near a solution. The contribution joins these two guarantees within a damped Newton method.

The global rate is O(1/k²), where k counts iterations, matching the rates of the regularized Newton methods discussed in the abstract. Locally, the quadratic rate matches the best known rate for second-order methods. The step-size formula is explicit and does not require solving an additional subproblem, making the rule straightforward to evaluate.

These guarantees hold under affine-invariant assumptions closely related to self-concordance; they are not claims about arbitrary optimization problems. Affine invariance means the assumptions respect changes of coordinates of the relevant kind. The paper also reports competitive performance against methods with similarly fast global guarantees. Its main result is therefore a simple step-size rule backed by strong, conditional convergence theory.
neurips-2022-a-damped-newton-method-achi.tldr: An explicit Newton step-size schedule achieves fast global and quadratic local convergence under affine-invariant assumptions related to self-concordance.

paragraphs: Document retrieval usually separates building an index from using that index to find relevant documents. This separation makes it difficult to optimize the index directly for retrieval quality. Neural Corpus Indexer brings the training and indexing stages into a single sequence-to-sequence neural network that generates relevant document identifiers from a query.

The model treats retrieval as identifier generation, so its decoder is central to selecting documents. The paper introduces a prefix-aware decoder with adaptive weights, together with query generation, document identifiers that carry semantic information, and consistency-based regularization. These components are tailored to improving recall within the unified retrieval system.

On two academic benchmarks, NCI improves over the best baseline reported in the study. The gains are 21.4% relative for Recall@1 on NQ320k and 16.8% relative for R-Precision on TriviaQA. These are relative improvements in distinct retrieval measures, rather than percentage-point gains. The results support the paper's central idea that learning to generate document identifiers can improve retrieval when indexing is trained toward the final task.
neurips-2022-a-neural-corpus-indexer-for.tldr: Neural Corpus Indexer learns to generate document identifiers directly from queries and improves retrieval performance on two benchmarks.

paragraphs: Comparing optimization methods requires more than presenting a promising theoretical result. Researchers must implement alternatives, run suitable experiments, and make those experiments understandable to others. The paper argues that growing numbers of methods, uneven evaluation practices, and repeated implementation work can leave numerical validation incomplete and lead to misleading conclusions.

Benchopt is a collaborative framework for automating, publishing, and reproducing optimization benchmarks. It supports experiments across programming languages and hardware architectures, giving researchers a common tool for running and sharing comparisons. Existing benchmarks can also be extended, so evaluation work can accumulate rather than requiring each group to rebuild the same experimental setup.

The paper demonstrates the framework with regularized logistic regression, Lasso, and ResNet18 image-classification training. These examples span different optimization tasks and illustrate how practical evaluation details can change the interpretation of leading methods. The contribution is both infrastructure for repeatable comparisons and evidence that careful benchmarking produces a more nuanced account of performance than a single headline result.
neurips-2022-benchopt-reproducible-effic.tldr: Benchopt provides shared infrastructure for running, extending, and reproducing optimization benchmarks across languages and hardware.

paragraphs: Brain networks represent regions of interest and the connections between them. This paper adapts Transformers to a specific feature of these data: the graphs have a fixed number and ordering of regions. That consistency allows each region's connection profile to serve as its features while supplying inexpensive information about its position in the network.

Attention learns strengths of interactions between regions that are useful for downstream prediction across individuals. The model also includes an Orthonormal Clustering Readout, combining self-supervised soft clustering with orthonormal projection. This component accounts for functional groups of regions that behave similarly and produces both distinguishable region representations and informative summaries of whole brain networks.

The authors also standardize the evaluation pipeline on the public ABIDE dataset to make comparisons between models more meaningful. Experiments report clear improvements on ABIDE and a restricted ABCD dataset. The findings support designing both attention and graph summarization around the consistent regional structure and functional organization present in these brain-network data.
neurips-2022-brain-network-transformer-b.tldr: Brain Network Transformer uses consistent region ordering and functional clustering to improve brain-network representations and prediction.

paragraphs: Approximate planning must account for errors in estimated action values. In discounted Markov decision processes, ordinary Approximate Policy Iteration has an error bound that scales with H² times the worst-case approximation error ε, where H is the effective horizon. Confident Approximate Policy Iteration reduces this dependence to Hε while retaining a deterministic stationary policy.

A stationary policy uses the same decision rule over time. Keeping this form distinguishes the result from an earlier route to similar accuracy using non-stationary policies. The improvement requires H times as much memory. The authors then apply CAPI to planning with local simulator access and d-dimensional linear value-function approximation, refining policies over a changing collection of states.

The resulting planner achieves approximately O(√d Hε) policy error using approximately O(dH⁴/ε²) simulator queries, with logarithmic factors suppressed. It combines an optimal accuracy bound with the best known query bound, which earlier algorithms achieved separately. The query bound is tight except in its dependence on H. These gains entail polynomial increases in memory and computation, including costs associated with the output policy.
neurips-2022-confident-approximate-polic.tldr: CAPI improves planning accuracy while retaining stationary policies and combines strong simulator-query bounds with increased memory and computation.

paragraphs: Model-based reinforcement learning chooses actions using a model of the environment. When that model generalizes poorly, uncertainty can make a sampled model unstable as a target for policy optimization. The paper connects this instability to aggressive policy changes and excessive exploration, especially when model-complexity measures become large even for simple nonlinear models.

Conservative Dual Policy Optimization addresses the problem through a Referential Update and a Conservative Update. It first optimizes a policy under a reference model, preserving an aspect of posterior sampling while providing greater stability. Maximizing expected model value then maintains a conservative range of randomness, aiming to control exploration without the harmful sampling behavior identified by the authors.

The theoretical results give CDPO the same regret as posterior-sampling reinforcement learning, together with monotonic policy improvement and global optimality. These claims concern the method's analyzed setting and do not establish a general finite-iteration solution for arbitrary nonlinear models. Empirical results also support its exploration efficiency. The contribution links more stable policy updates with both exploration guarantees and observed performance.
neurips-2022-conservative-dual-policy-op.tldr: CDPO combines reference-model and conservative policy updates to stabilize exploration while retaining theoretical regret and policy-improvement guarantees.

paragraphs: A physical system can change continuously while some quantities remain constant. Discovering these constants of motion helps explain the system's dynamics, but usually requires mathematical analysis performed by hand. This paper presents a neural network that learns both how a system evolves and which quantities remain conserved, using data as the basis for both tasks.

The discovered constants also contribute to the network's predictions. By exploiting them, the method can make better predictions of the system's dynamics. This connects learning a useful physical description with learning to forecast motion. The abstract further states that the approach can handle a wider range of systems than neural networks based on Hamiltonian formulations.

The authors also identify a possible diagnostic use for the learning process itself. How training progresses can indicate the number of constants of motion in a system. That indication could help researchers investigating unfamiliar physical systems, alongside the learned dynamics and conserved quantities. It is presented as a potentially useful signal, rather than a guaranteed exact count for every system.
neurips-2022-constants-of-motion-network.tldr: A neural network jointly learns physical dynamics and conserved quantities, using those quantities to improve predictions.

paragraphs: Image-restoration Transformers face a tradeoff between broad interaction and computational cost. Global attention is expensive, while attention restricted to small square windows limits direct communication between windows. Cross Aggregation Transformer addresses this problem by changing the geometry of the regions over which attention operates and adding mechanisms for exchanging information.

Its Rectangle-Window Self-Attention uses horizontal and vertical rectangular windows in different attention heads at the same time. These elongated regions expand the attention area and aggregate information across different windows. An additional Axial-Shift operation supports further interaction between windows, helping the model connect image information beyond a single local square.

CAT also introduces a Locality Complementary Module that brings convolutional biases, including locality and translation invariance, into the Transformer. This couples broader interactions with sensitivity to nearby image structure. Experiments report improvements over recent leading methods on several image-restoration applications. The results support the combined design: wider communication through attention together with local structure supplied by the complementary module.
neurips-2022-cross-aggregation-transform.tldr: CAT combines rectangular attention windows, window shifts, and convolutional structure to improve image restoration.

paragraphs: Training large foundation models commonly relies on specialized GPU clusters with fast, uniform connections. This paper investigates training with model parallelism across decentralized devices connected by slower, heterogeneous networks. The challenge extends beyond dividing training examples: different pieces of the model's computation must be assigned to devices whose communication conditions vary.

The core contribution is a scheduling algorithm that allocates small computational units, called tasklets, across the available GPUs. A formal cost model describes the allocation problem, and an evolutionary algorithm searches for an allocation strategy. Together, these components make device placement and communication costs explicit parts of organizing foundation-model training.

The experiments simulate geographically distributed training scenarios using real-world network measurements. In the most extreme reported scenario, representing eight cities across three continents, the approach is 4.8 times faster than prior leading training systems. This is a result for that simulated setting, rather than a general speedup for every network. It shows the potential value of scheduling designed specifically for heterogeneous, lower-bandwidth environments.
neurips-2022-decentralized-training-of-f.tldr: A scheduling method improves decentralized foundation-model training by allocating computation around heterogeneous devices and network connections.

paragraphs: Belief Propagation solves reasoning problems by passing messages through a graphical model. For constraint optimization, mixing old and new messages through damping can improve performance, but a fixed damping factor is laborious to tune. Giving every neighboring variable equal influence can also limit how effectively the algorithm explores possible solutions.

Deep Attentive Belief Propagation learns how to compose messages during the reasoning process. It takes the factor graph and current messages as inputs, combining gated recurrent units, graph attention networks, and multi-head attention to determine dynamic weights and damping factors. This makes both the influence of neighboring information and the balance between old and new messages adaptive.

The training method uses a smoothed solution cost as a self-supervised signal, avoiding expensive labels. Efficient online learning is also presented as a way to avoid the out-of-distribution issue encountered by existing neural BP variants. Extensive experiments report significant improvements over leading baselines. The paper's contribution is a learned control mechanism integrated into message passing, together with a training approach tied directly to solution quality.
neurips-2022-deep-attentive-belief-propa.tldr: DABP learns adaptive message weights and damping for belief propagation using self-supervised online training.

paragraphs: Neural solvers have shown promise on difficult graph optimization problems, but many reinforcement-learning approaches struggle to scale beyond a few hundred nodes. Building solutions sequentially or repeatedly refining discrete candidates can be costly. DIMES addresses this scalability problem by changing how the solver represents and searches over candidate solutions.

The method introduces a compact continuous space that parameterizes a distribution over discrete solutions. Training can then adjust that distribution using REINFORCE, while drawing many candidate solutions in parallel. The same representation supports fine-tuning. This shifts the learning process toward controlling a sampleable distribution, providing a route to stable training and large-scale parallel sampling.

DIMES also uses meta-learning to produce effective parameter initializations for the fine-tuning stage. The goal is to make subsequent adaptation begin from a useful learned starting point. Experiments report that DIMES outperforms recent reinforcement-learning solvers on large benchmark datasets for Traveling Salesman and Maximal Independent Set problems. These results support its scalability strategy without establishing exact solutions to arbitrary instances of these difficult problems.
neurips-2022-dimes-a-differentiable-meta.tldr: DIMES represents candidate solutions through a compact continuous distribution, enabling parallel sampling and meta-learned fine-tuning for large graph optimization problems.

paragraphs: Deep ensembles estimate uncertainty by measuring how much separately trained neural networks disagree. This disagreement can help identify unfamiliar inputs, but its theoretical basis is less clear than its empirical usefulness. The paper asks what produces predictive variance and how those sources influence the uncertainty signal an ensemble provides.

The analysis begins with wide networks in simplified linear training regimes, where the neural tangent kernel describes functions learned through gradient descent. Within this setting, the authors distinguish two sources of noise that produce different inductive biases in predictive variance at initialization. Separating these sources helps explain why ensemble disagreement has a particular structure.

The authors then show theoretically and empirically that both sources influence trained nonlinear ensembles, using toy models and realistic settings. They also propose practical interventions that remove part of the noise and report improved detection of out-of-distribution inputs. The findings connect a simplified analytical account to trained networks, showing that the ingredients of predictive variance can be adjusted to improve its usefulness as an uncertainty signal.
neurips-2022-disentangling-the-predictiv.tldr: The paper identifies two noise sources shaping ensemble uncertainty and uses that analysis to improve unfamiliar-input detection.

paragraphs: Constrained Markov games describe multiple players making decisions over time while obeying behavioral constraints. Although Nash equilibria exist in this setting, computing them presents a major complexity barrier. This paper proposes a surrogate correlated-equilibrium notion that can be computed in polynomial time and studies how constraints change its underlying structure.

A central result is that the associated Lagrangian has zero duality gap. This connects the constrained problem with its dual formulation and supports a primal-dual algorithm with a convergence guarantee. The authors also show that the structure of permissible equilibrium modifications differs fundamentally from the unconstrained setting, so constraints require more than directly reusing the existing formulation.

For the proposed algorithm, both the duality gap and constraint violation decrease at rate O(1/√T). With V-learning used for the primal update, the sample-complexity bound is O(H⁹|S||A|²ε⁻⁴) for an approximate equilibrium with ε duality gap. The contribution combines a tractable surrogate solution concept with quantitative guarantees on approaching equilibrium and satisfying constraints.
neurips-2022-finding-correlated-equilibr.tldr: A surrogate correlated equilibrium enables a provably convergent primal-dual method for constrained Markov games.

paragraphs: Stochastic gradient descent can behave differently as the dimension of a learning problem grows. This paper derives limiting descriptions of selected summary statistics of constant-step-size SGD. Tracking a finite collection of quantities allows the analysis to describe effective dynamics without following every coordinate of an increasingly large parameter vector.

The framework accommodates choices of summary statistics, initialization, and step size. Depending on those choices, the limiting behavior can be described by ordinary or stochastic differential equations. Below a critical step-size scaling, the effective dynamics matches gradient flow for the population loss. At the critical scaling, an additional correction appears and changes the phase diagram.

The authors apply the framework to spiked matrix and tensor estimation and to two-layer classification networks for Gaussian mixture models. These examples reveal multiple characteristic convergence times and a probability of reaching suboptimal solutions that remains bounded away from zero under random initialization. The results show why initialization and step-size scaling can fundamentally alter high-dimensional learning dynamics, including fluctuations near fixed points.
neurips-2022-high-dimensional-limit-theo.tldr: High-dimensional limit theorems reveal how SGD's effective dynamics changes with initialization, tracked statistics, and critical step-size scaling.

paragraphs: Accelerated MRI reconstructs anatomy from measurements that are incomplete and noisy. Convolutional networks perform well at this task, but have difficulty representing long-range image relationships. Transformers offer a way to model those relationships, yet their computation and memory requirements become especially demanding when high resolution and fine detail must both be preserved.

HUMUS-Net combines convolutions and Transformers in an unrolled, multi-scale architecture. Convolutional blocks extract high-resolution features, while a Transformer-based multi-scale feature extractor refines lower-resolution features. The network then synthesizes information from both levels into a high-resolution reconstruction. This division assigns detailed feature extraction and broader feature refinement to complementary components.

The authors report a new state of the art on fastMRI, described in the abstract as the largest publicly available MRI dataset. They also evaluate the network on two other MRI datasets and use fine-grained ablations to assess its design. The findings support combining efficient convolutional processing with attention across scales as a practical architecture for the reconstruction task studied.
neurips-2022-humus-net-hybrid-unrolled-m.tldr: HUMUS-Net combines high-resolution convolutional features with lower-resolution Transformer processing to improve accelerated MRI reconstruction.

paragraphs: Sketches compress high-dimensional vectors into smaller representations that still support useful estimates, particularly when the vectors are sparse or nearly sparse. They are valuable in distributed and streaming computation. Differential privacy can be added by introducing noise calibrated to the sketch's sensitivity, but the resulting estimation error determines how useful the private sketch remains.

This paper gives an improved error analysis for CountSketch made private with Gaussian noise. Its main finding is that the privacy-utility tradeoff is essentially as favorable as one could hope for. The estimation error is almost the same as ordinary CountSketch error plus the noise needed to privatize the original high-dimensional vector.

Crucially, this near-ideal tradeoff is independent of CountSketch's number of repetitions. The result sharpens the understanding of an existing private sketch construction rather than introducing a different compression method. Differential privacy's post-processing property also means that all estimates derived from the private sketch can be released within its privacy budget, making the accuracy analysis relevant to multiple downstream uses.
neurips-2022-improved-utility-analysis-o.tldr: An improved analysis shows Gaussian-private CountSketch achieves a near-ideal privacy-accuracy tradeoff independent of its number of repetitions.

paragraphs: Large image-text models learn from enormous collections of paired images and language, including noisy data that does not require carefully produced labels. Studying these models at their intended scale requires billions of pairs. LAION-5B addresses the lack of openly available data at that scale by providing a resource for broader research participation.

The dataset contains 5.85 billion image-text pairs filtered using CLIP, including 2.32 billion pairs with English text. The authors demonstrate successful replication and fine-tuning of models such as CLIP, GLIDE, and Stable Diffusion using the dataset. These demonstrations establish that the collection can support substantial language-vision modeling work, beyond simply offering a large catalog of paired data.

The release also includes nearest-neighbor indices, a web interface for exploring the collection and generating subsets, and detection scores for watermarks, NSFW content, and toxic content. These supporting tools help researchers navigate and select from the dataset. The contribution therefore combines scale, open availability, demonstrated model-training uses, and infrastructure for working with the collection.
neurips-2022-laion-5b-an-open-large-scal.tldr: LAION-5B opens access to 5.85 billion CLIP-filtered image-text pairs and tools for exploring and using them in multimodal research.

paragraphs: A classifier can struggle because of the conditions under which an example was captured, such as poor lighting in an image. This paper studies recourse that changes those environmental conditions so the instance can be captured again. RecourseNet learns to recommend settings intended to make the resulting instance easier for a classifier to predict accurately.

The recommendation problem is difficult because the physical process that generates a recaptured instance is not assumed to be available. The best environment can also depend on the particular instance: an object's shape may affect which camera angle is useful. A single fixed recommendation therefore cannot express all the instance-dependent choices the method seeks to learn.

The proposed three-level training method learns a classifier suited to prediction under recourse, learns a recourse predictor even when good-environment examples are limited, and learns when to trigger recourse selectively. That trigger depends on whether classifier confidence is likely to improve. The contribution is a coordinated learning framework for classification and environment recommendations; the abstract does not equate increased confidence with guaranteed correctness.
neurips-2022-learning-recourse-on-instan.tldr: RecourseNet learns instance-specific changes to capture conditions and selectively recommends recapture when classifier confidence is likely to improve.

paragraphs: When classes are unevenly represented, training examples can contribute unequally to a useful classifier. Re-weighting addresses this by assigning different importance to examples in the training loss. Many existing approaches learn these weights through a costly two-level optimization process involving the classifier and a separate meta set.

This paper instead frames weight learning as matching distributions with optimal transport. The training samples form an imbalanced distribution, with their weights represented as probability mass. A balanced distribution is constructed from the meta set. Learning then adjusts the training weights to minimize the optimal-transport distance between the two distributions.

This distributional formulation removes the dependence of weight learning on the classifier at each iteration. It changes the optimization task used to obtain example weights while retaining their role in addressing class imbalance. Experiments cover image, text, and point-cloud datasets and report state-of-the-art results in many cases. Those findings support optimal transport as a useful approach across the tested data types, without implying that it wins on every imbalanced classification problem.
neurips-2022-learning-to-re-weight-examp.tldr: Optimal-transport-based re-weighting learns example importance by matching an imbalanced training distribution to a balanced meta distribution.

paragraphs: Teams can achieve outcomes beyond what their members could accomplish separately, but dividing the reward raises questions of contribution and cooperation. Cooperative game theory provides concepts such as the Shapley value for contribution-based allocation and the Core for reducing incentives to leave a team. Computing these solutions can be difficult even in restricted settings.

Neural Payoff Machines learn to propose allocations by distilling cooperative game-theoretic solutions into neural networks. The approach aims to retain the usefulness of fair and stable allocation concepts while replacing repeated expensive solution computations with predictions from a trained model. Fairness and stability here refer to the game-theoretic concepts motivating the learned outputs.

The authors show that the resulting models can generalize to games far from their training distribution and predict solutions involving more players than were present during training. They also identify explainable AI as an application: the framework can accelerate Shapley-value computations across many instances. These findings support learned approximation as a way to make computationally demanding allocation concepts more accessible.
neurips-2022-neural-payoff-machines-pred.tldr: Neural Payoff Machines learn to predict game-theoretic reward allocations and can generalize to unfamiliar games and larger teams.

paragraphs: Satisfiability asks whether logical constraints admit a valid assignment, while model counting asks how many such assignments exist. NSNet treats both tasks through probabilistic inference. Its graph neural network parameterizes belief propagation in a latent space, keeping a probabilistic interpretation for its hidden representations and giving the framework an interpretable internal structure.

For SAT, NSNet estimates marginal probabilities across satisfying solutions instead of directly predicting one complete assignment. The authors empirically find this target more feasible for neural networks to learn. The estimated marginals then guide rounding and stochastic local search to generate a satisfying assignment, connecting probabilistic predictions with a discrete solution procedure.

For #SAT, the learning objective changes to approximate counting through the Bethe approximation of the partition function. This lets one general framework serve two related but distinct tasks. Evaluations on multiple SAT and #SAT datasets report competitive inference accuracy and time efficiency. The results support learning probabilistically meaningful intermediate quantities as a useful route to both solution search and approximate counting.
neurips-2022-nsnet-a-general-neural-prob.tldr: NSNet combines neural belief propagation with probabilistic objectives to solve satisfiability and approximate model-counting tasks.

paragraphs: Imaging inverse problems reconstruct images from measurements using both a physical measurement model and prior knowledge about images. Plug-and-Play and Regularization by Denoising methods combine these ingredients through fixed-point computations. Deep equilibrium learning allows the image prior to be trained end to end by differentiating implicitly through the fixed-point equations.

Implicit differentiation avoids storing intermediate activation values, but it does not remove every computational bottleneck. Processing the measurement model can still require computation and memory that grow with the total number of measurements. ODER addresses this remaining burden by using stochastic approximations of the measurement models within deep equilibrium learning.

The paper provides theoretical analysis of ODER's convergence and its ability to approximate the traditional deep equilibrium approach. Numerical results across three imaging applications suggest potential reductions in training and testing complexity. The findings are framed as evidence of possible efficiency gains, rather than a universal performance guarantee. The contribution targets measurement-related costs while retaining the fixed-point learning framework used to optimize image priors.
neurips-2022-online-deep-equilibrium-lea.tldr: ODER uses stochastic measurement-model approximations to potentially reduce the cost of deep equilibrium learning for image reconstruction.

paragraphs: The paper asks how to draw an exact sample from an unknown discrete distribution when only comparison outcomes are available. Each observation supplies a compared set and a winner drawn from the target distribution conditioned on that set. The main focus is pairwise comparisons, where each observed set contains two elements.

The authors first construct a Markov chain whose stationary distribution is the desired target and use Coupling from the Past to obtain exact samples. However, this route can require exponentially many observations in natural cases because its cost depends on the target distribution's structure. Exactness alone therefore does not ensure an efficient sampling procedure.

The main contribution removes that structural dependence from the sampling complexity. An efficient comparison-learning algorithm supplies a good approximation to the target distribution, which is then used to speed up a parameterized Markov chain. Crucially, the final samples remain exact even though the acceleration uses an approximation. The authors also suggest that this general technique for accelerating chains with approximately known stationary distributions may have independent value.
neurips-2022-perfect-sampling-from-pairw.tldr: An approximate distribution learned from pairwise comparisons accelerates a Markov-chain procedure that still produces exact samples.

paragraphs: Exploration in reinforcement learning often rewards encountering novel states, but novelty is difficult to define in complex visual environments. This paper measures novelty using semantically meaningful abstractions shaped by natural language. The approach uses pretrained vision-language representations to describe states in terms that can be more relevant to the task.

The representations come from models pretrained on natural image-captioning datasets. The authors show that they guide meaningful exploration and improve performance in simulated 3D environments. They investigate language's contribution by comparing pretrained representations, a language oracle, and several ablations, aiming to understand how the abstraction influences exploration behavior.

The evaluation includes both on-policy and off-policy reinforcement-learning algorithms and two distinct task domains. One emphasizes recognizing and manipulating everyday objects; the other requires navigation through a large world. Results across these settings suggest that language-shaped representations could benefit different algorithms and agents. The broader implication remains a possibility supported by these experiments, while the demonstrated gains concern the tested simulated environments.
neurips-2022-semantic-exploration-from-l.tldr: Pretrained language-shaped visual representations make novelty more task-relevant and improve exploration in tested 3D reinforcement-learning environments.

paragraphs: Gradient-boosted decision trees are effective on many data-science tasks, but training can scale poorly when each example has a highly multidimensional output. This paper focuses on that multioutput setting. It targets the computation used to choose tree splits, an operation that must compare possible ways of dividing the training data.

SketchBoost accelerates training by approximating the scoring function used to identify the best split. The method therefore reduces work within tree construction while continuing to learn a boosted tree model. The proposed techniques are implemented in SketchBoost and integrated into Py-Boost, the authors' customizable Python-based GPU implementation of gradient-boosted decision trees.

The numerical study reports training speedups reaching more than 40 times, with comparable or sometimes better predictive performance. That figure describes the upper end of the reported gains, rather than an expected acceleration on every task. The findings show that approximate split scoring can offer substantial computational savings in the studied multioutput problems without necessarily sacrificing the quality of the resulting predictions.
neurips-2022-sketchboost-fast-gradient-b.tldr: SketchBoost approximates tree-split scores to accelerate multioutput gradient boosting, with reported speedups exceeding 40 times in some cases.
